_leadership_summary:
The national score climbed from about 3.2 in January to 3.36 in August, and the gain came from tier migration rather than a broad lift in performance. Stores that were already struggling or already strong mostly stayed where they were on score; what changed is how many crossed the tier lines. Roughly a quarter of the bottom tier moved up, and the top tier grew by about a third, from around 840 stores to over 1,100. That is real progress, but it is fragile. Twice as many stores moved up as moved down, yet more than 350 top-tier stores slipped a tier, so the top is being refilled as fast as it is leaking. The movement was led by Win Score and Hutbot Ontime, which rose steadily, while Brand and FSCC stayed flat or drifted lower. Speed dipped through spring and only rebounded sharply in August, so we should treat that recovery as unproven until it holds for a second month.

Zone results are encouraging but uneven. Florida Peninsula leads and roughly halved its bottom tier. Texas North/Oklahoma, Upper Midwest, Great Lakes East and Texas South all gained 0.2 to 0.3 or more, so improvement is not confined to the strongest zones. Gulf Central and Deep South are flat, and Deep South still carries the largest bottom tier of any zone and saw it grow. Southwest/Rockies and Cellesha Steel barely reduced their bottom tiers despite score gains, and Ohio Valley remains the lowest-scoring zone even as it improves. Several zones are also growing their top tier by 50% or more from a small base, which will be hard to defend.

Portfolio health is a middle-heavy picture: about 60% of stores sit in the middle tier, a quarter in the top, and about a sixth in the bottom. The binding constraint changes by tier and explains why one national message will not work. In the bottom tier, Win Score is the limiting factor for two-thirds of stores, and Speed is a distant second. In the middle tier, Win Score still binds about half the time, with Speed and Brand both meaningful. At the top, the constraint is evenly split across Win Score, Speed and Brand, which means the stores we most want to protect have no single weak spot to fix. Exposure is concentrated: about 300 stores are defaulting, 30 more are at risk, and nearly 400 bottom-tier stores are on watch. Franchisee results are polarized, with several operators near 4.0 and a handful of multi-unit groups under the 2.2 mark, all under the same two directors. Finally, the link between five-star scores and sales trends is weak, so we should not assume tier gains will show up in comps without evidence.

The national priority is to make Speed the single operational focus. It is the constraint that shows up in every tier, it was the one component that fell for most of the year, and August's rebound is our opening to lock it in. Concretely, I recommend three actions: pair the Speed push with Win Score coaching in the middle tier, where the largest volume of upward movement is available; direct field leadership to the Deep South, Southwest/Rockies and Ohio Valley bottom-tier stores and the low-scoring multi-unit franchisees for hands-on intervention; and put the defaulting and at-risk stores on a named-owner recovery plan with monthly review. Success by year-end looks like Speed holding above August's level for three consecutive months and fewer top-tier stores slipping back down.

_brief.summary:
Bootcamps are landing. Sixty workshops reached 448 stores in August, and of the 378 stores with a follow-up read, about two in three (248) improved, with average scores rising from 2.88 to 3.11. Dustin Patton stands out: ten workshops last month, 80 stores coached, and the strongest lift of any zone. Derron Spencer leads year-to-date volume with 23 workshops and has nine more booked. Danielle Hudson pairs 20 workshops with the biggest overall gain, from 3.07 to 3.37. One caution: lift estimates are only as reliable as the comparison, so we should treat them as strong directional evidence.
Sales are moving the right way. Last month, four of five quintiles posted positive same-store sales, against negative results across the board year to date. The top quintile leads at about +1.7% sales and +3.5% transactions. The bottom quintile is the drag, at roughly -1.9% sales and -0.9% transactions, with speed of service the weakest score (1.67). Traffic, not ticket, is driving the story, though the 5-Star to growth correlation is modest (0.11), so it is one lever among several.
Franchisee momentum is real: national average moved from 3.19 in January to 3.36 in August, and Tier 1 stores fell from 1,006 to 772. Sergio Villasenor (+0.29) and Sarah Heitz (+0.25) are rising fast on the back of double-digit Tier 1 reductions. Worth watching are Paul Inacio and Jesse White, both flat, and Derron Spencer, whose heavy coaching volume has yet to show in his average (+0.08). Our OAs and FOPs ran 60 workshops, coached 448 stores, and helped fewer stores land in Tier 1 while sales turned positive.
